lesson.title: The BINS Checklist: When Does a Situation Count as Binomial?
lesson.summary: Before you can use any binomial formula, a situation has to pass four specific tests. This chapter walks through each one and shows how to check them with real numbers.
lesson.body:
You already know what a binomial setting looks like in general terms: repeated trials with two outcomes. This chapter turns that general idea into a checklist you can actually run against a real problem, because plenty of situations look binomial at first glance and then fall apart under closer inspection. Four conditions have to hold, and a handy way to remember them is the acronym BINS: Binary, Independent, Number fixed, Same probability.

Binary means each trial has exactly two possible outcomes, usually labeled success and failure. Independent means the outcome of one trial gives you no information about the outcome of any other trial. Number fixed means you decide on the number of trials, n, in advance, before you see any data. Same probability means the probability of success, p, stays constant from trial to trial.

The independence condition is the one that trips people up most often, especially when sampling from a real, finite population without replacement. Strictly speaking, drawing people one at a time out of a population without putting them back changes the makeup of what's left, so the probability of success shifts slightly with every draw. Statisticians handle this with the 10% condition: if your sample size is less than 10% of the population size, that shift is small enough to ignore, and you can treat the trials as approximately independent.

Consider a pollster who samples 40 people from a population of 5,000 registered voters to ask whether they support a ballot measure. Ten percent of 5,000 is 500, and the sample size of 40 is well under that, so the 10% condition is satisfied. Combined with a binary yes or no response, a fixed sample size decided before polling began, and a support rate that stays essentially constant across such a small slice of the population, this situation passes all four BINS conditions and can be modeled as binomial.

Now compare that to a teacher who draws 5 students without replacement from a class of 30 to ask whether they prefer online homework. Ten percent of 30 is only 3, and the sample size of 5 exceeds that. Removing even one student changes the class's remaining preference rate noticeably, since 1 out of 29 is a much bigger shift than 1 out of 4,999. The trials here are not close enough to independent, so a binomial model would be a poor approximation, even though the situation is binary and the sample size is fixed.

Checking these four conditions is not busywork. Every formula in the chapters ahead, the distribution itself, the shortcut for computing probabilities, the mean, the standard deviation, all assume BINS holds. Skip the check and the numbers those formulas produce can be badly wrong.
